chosen.premise: If Tauros cannot find an opponent, it charges thick trees and knocks them down just to calm itself.
chosen.hook: What does Tauros do when nobody wants to fight it?
chosen.visualIdea: An empty field frustrates Tauros until it targets a tree, charges, and leaves it crashing down.
chosen.note: An unusually memorable contradiction: Tauros needs to fight so badly that it attacks trees to calm down. The premise, hook, and visuals align exactly with the Ruby and Emerald entries.

candidates.premise: Tauros whips its three tails to heighten its fighting will—and to warn that a charge is seconds away.
candidates.hook: Tauros doesn't just charge. It announces the attack with three tails.
candidates.visualIdea: Three tails lash faster as a warning meter fills, then Tauros launches into a full-speed charge.
candidates.note: The three-tail warning is highly specific to Tauros, clearly documented in multiple entries, and naturally creates a strong animated escalation.

candidates.premise: In Tauros herds, the boss is the one with the longest, thickest, most battle-scarred horns.
candidates.hook: Tauros chooses its herd boss by reading the horns.
candidates.visualIdea: Three Tauros silhouettes compare horn length, thickness, and scars before one becomes the herd leader.
candidates.note: The three-part horn criterion is concrete and easy to show. It is strongly supported, though herd dominance is a somewhat familiar animal-behavior angle.

candidates.premise: Tauros keeps the same 1.4-meter height across four builds, but its weight and types change dramatically.
candidates.hook: Tauros changes its build without changing its height.
candidates.visualIdea: Four Tauros forms line up at equal height while labels reveal weights from 85 to 115 kilograms and new types.
candidates.note: The equal 1.4-meter height versus 85–115 kilogram range and changing types make a clean visual comparison. It is data-driven, though the height contrast is less emotionally compelling than Tauros's behavior.

candidates.premise: Once Tauros starts running, it will not stop until it hits something.
candidates.hook: Tauros has only one way to end a sprint: impact.
candidates.visualIdea: Tauros accelerates across an empty path while a stop button fails, ending only when it hits a target.
candidates.note: The hard stopping rule is striking and directly supported by two entries. It is slightly less distinctive than the tree-rampage premise because unstoppable charging is already central to Tauros's general identity.

candidates.premise: Tauros can be fierce, calmer in Alola, and too volatile for riders in Galar.
candidates.hook: The same Pokémon has three completely different attitudes by region.
candidates.visualIdea: A map switches from calm Alolan Tauros to volatile Galarian Tauros that throws off a rider.
candidates.note: Regional personality differences are interesting and supported, but 'three completely different attitudes' oversimplifies the entries and does not establish a precise rule for why the temper changes.

rounds.request: None; this angle is strong enough to lead the episode. Stronger alternatives would need an equally unusual Tauros-specific behavior, a precise rule or contradiction, direct Pokédex support, and a visual escalation that pays off immediately.
